newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens flock to elections after bloody conflict.
newsitem.headline: Chechens flock to elections after bloody conflict.

text.p: Chechens packed polling stations on Monday in presidential and parliamentary elections that will reinforce the mainly Moslem region's demands for independence from Russia following a nearly two-year war.
Election officials described the turnout as heavy in both the devastated regional capital Grozny and in rural areas on a cold and clear winter's day.

In some places more than 100 hundred voters queued up, pushing and shoving towards voting booths. Some wore traditional sheepskin hats but few people on the streets brandished guns, even though the region is still awash with weapons.
"We need an end to chaos and these elections will put us on the road to a better life," said Musa Sagalayev, 45, after casting his ballot at polling station number seven in Grozny.

Aslan Maskhadov, who as commander of a small guerrilla army forced Russian troops into a humiliating withdrawal after 21 months of bitter fighting over independence, is the clear frontrunner among the 13 presidential challengers.

Straw polls last week suggested Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet army colonel, could win outright with more than 50 percent of the vote. If no candidate wins outright, a run-off will be held in two weeks.

Casting his ballot at a old dairy collective farm 20 km (12 miles) northwest of Grozny, Maskhadov predicted he would win 60 percent of the vote. He pledged to "bring order" to Chechnya as his first step and to develop normal ties with Russia.
"We need to develop normal ties so that we won't have to wage war anymore," said the grey-haired commander, dressed in a sheepskin hat.
His main rivals are acting President Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, field commander Shamil Basayev and rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov. Maskhadov appears to be Moscow's preferred choice.

Basayev, 32, led a bloody raid on the southern Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995, and is a wanted man in Russia. His election would be a nightmare for the Kremlin, already humiliated by the failure to defeat Chechnya's guerrilla army.
Casting his vote in the snow-clad mountain village of Vedeno, Basayev forecast his own victory and warned Russia it would "collapse" if it failed to accept Chechen independence.

Seventy-two international observers were watching voting on behalf of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). Some said they were surprised by the high turnout and the smooth way the poll was proceeding.
"It is obvious that they (the Chechens) want to show Russia and the whole world that they are capable of organising democratic elections," said one Scandinavian observer.
Chechen leaders, worried that violence could disrupt the voting, have taken extensive security measures.
All the main candidates have pledged to turn the de facto autonomy secured by last month's Russian troop withdrawal into full sovereignty after 200 years of Russian and Soviet rule.
But the Kremlin, fearing instability on its southern flank and unrest among other minorities, has ruled out secession.
Maskhadov says he is determined to seek reparations from Moscow. Tens of thousands of civilians died in the war, which President Boris Yeltsin says was a mistake.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Saturday he would work with any elected leader. But various complaints about the voting have given some observers the impression that Moscow may be preparing to question the ballot's legitimacy.

Yeltsin agreed to elections as part of a peace deal last August which deferred solving the dispute over Chechnya's political status for five years. Maskhadov and the other main contenders now say they will not delay negotiations any longer.
Some half a million voters -- about half the pre-war population -- may be eligible. Precise data are not available.
As many as 60,000 refugees outside Chechnya are expected to vote at polling stations set up near the borders.
Polls were due to close at 8 p.m. (1700 GMT) and first results were expected as early as Monday night. Some 850 candidates are also standing for 63 local assembly seats.
